title: Who Is Sal Khan? The Son of Immigrants From India and Bangladesh Who Became the World's Teacher — and Is Now Building a $10,000 AI College
excerpt: From tutoring his cousin on a Yahoo notepad to launching a college backed by Google and Microsoft, Sal Khan turned a free education mission into a global movement.
body:
In 2004, a hedge fund analyst in Boston opened a Yahoo notepad to tutor his teenage cousin in math over the internet. He had no plan to change education. He was just trying to help Nadia pass seventh-grade unit conversion. Two decades later, that analyst's free video lessons have been watched more than two billion times, his nonprofit platform reaches tens of millions of learners in 190 countries, and he is now building a college that could cost less than what most American families spend on a single semester.

His name is Sal Khan. And if you have school-age children, there is a decent chance they already know him better than you do.

From Metairie to MIT

Salman Amin Khan was born on October 11, 1976, in Metairie, a suburb of New Orleans, Louisiana. His father, Fakhrul Amin Khan, was a physician from the village of Rahmatpur in Barishal, Bangladesh. His mother, Masuda Khan, is from Murshidabad in West Bengal, India. The family's roots run deep: Khan's paternal grandfather, Abdul Wahab Khan, served as Pakistan's third Speaker of the National Assembly.

But prestige did not translate into comfort. Khan's parents divorced when he was two. His father died when Sal was thirteen. His mother raised him on roughly $16,000 a year — he knew the figure precisely because he did her taxes to apply for financial aid.

At Grace King High School, where "a few classmates were fresh out of jail and others were bound for top universities," as Khan later recalled, he played guitar in a heavy metal band, drew cartoons for the school paper, and quietly took college math courses at the University of New Orleans. He graduated as valedictorian in 1994 and headed to MIT.

There, he earned three degrees by 1998: a bachelor's in mathematics, a combined bachelor's in electrical engineering and computer science, and a master's in electrical engineering. He later added an MBA from Harvard Business School.

A Cousin's Math Problem Changes Everything

After Harvard, Khan joined Connective Capital Management as a hedge fund analyst. The work was lucrative. But in 2004, his cousin Nadia needed help with math, and the family's expectations kicked in. He began tutoring her remotely using Yahoo's doodle notepad. Word spread. More cousins asked. Then friends of cousins.

""I felt like the whole point was to not have a personality distract from the math," he said."

By 2006, Khan started posting short, unpolished videos to YouTube — just a black screen, simple graphics, and his voice walking through problems. He deliberately stayed off camera. "I felt like the whole point was to not have a personality distract from the math," he said.

The videos caught fire. Strangers began leaving thank-you notes in the comments. A mother wrote that Khan's tutorials had helped her two disabled children and that her family was praying for his. By 2009, the volume of messages made it impossible to ignore: Khan quit his hedge fund job and committed to Khan Academy full-time.

"I didn't come from a traditional Desi family of engineers pushing their kids. My dad was a doctor — that's why my parents settled in New Orleans. But I didn't really know him."

A Nonprofit in a World of Unicorns

Khan Academy grew explosively, but Khan made a choice that Silicon Valley found strange: he kept it a nonprofit. No ads. No paywalls. No premium tiers. The mission was radical in its simplicity — a free, world-class education for anyone, anywhere.

The model attracted heavyweight backing. The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation became one of the academy's biggest supporters. Google awarded a $2 million grant. In 2012, Bill Gates said publicly: "I've used Khan Academy with my kids, and I'm amazed at the breadth of Sal's subject expertise and his ability to make complicated topics understandable." That same year, Time named Khan one of the 100 most influential people in the world, and Forbes put him on its cover with the tagline "The $1 Trillion Opportunity."

Today, Khan Academy offers content across mathematics, science, computing, economics, history, and test preparation. Its partnership with the College Board provides free SAT practice to millions. More than 155 million users have registered on the platform. Stanford AI researcher Andrew Ng has credited Khan as an inspiration for the founding of Coursera.

AI, Google, and a $10,000 College Degree

Khan has not rested on what made him famous. In recent years, he has leaned hard into artificial intelligence as an educational tool. Khanmigo, the platform's AI-powered tutor launched in 2023, uses large language models to engage students in Socratic dialogue rather than simply handing them answers. A recent Google partnership is now integrating Gemini into Khan Academy's Writing Coach and an upcoming Reading Coach, designed for grades 5 through 12.

But the most ambitious move is the Khan TED Institute. Announced in 2026, it is a joint venture with TED and testing giant ETS that aims to offer a fully accredited Bachelor of Science degree in Applied AI — for under $10,000 total. That is less than many Americans pay for a single semester at a state university. The curriculum is being co-designed with Google, Microsoft, McKinsey, Bain, and Accenture. Coursework is online and asynchronous. Credentials are competency-based, not seat-time-based.

"We think there are many good reasons to go to a traditional university, but not everyone has access to those opportunities," Khan said. "The world is changing very, very, very fast."

The institute emerged after Khan became TED's Vision Steward in October 2025, succeeding Chris Anderson, who described Khan as someone who "has proven that technology and learning can serve humanity at scale — without losing integrity or heart."

What the Research Shows

Khan Academy's effectiveness has moved beyond anecdote. A January 2026 NBER working paper studied 83 residential government middle schools in Uttar Pradesh, India, in a randomized controlled trial. All schools had access to Khan Academy, but treatment schools received dedicated lab supervisors to ensure consistent, high-quality implementation. The result: mathematics achievement rose by nearly half a standard deviation over 31 weeks — a massive effect size by education research standards — with gains spread broadly across achievement levels.

The study's conclusion was pointed: the bottleneck in scaling educational technology is not the software or the content. It is the organizational structure around it.

Why He Matters to the Diaspora

Khan received India's Padma Shri in 2016 — one of the few Americans of South Asian descent to be honored with the civilian award. He holds honorary doctorates from Harvard, Dartmouth, and Carnegie Mellon. He lives in Mountain View, California, with his wife, physician Umaima Marvi, and their three children.

His story speaks to something specific about the Indian and Bangladeshi diaspora experience: the immigrant family that sacrifices everything for education, the child who absorbs that ethic and then turns it outward, offering the same access to millions who never had it. Khan did not build a billion-dollar company. He built something that might matter more — a platform where a student in rural Uttar Pradesh and a teenager in suburban Louisiana can watch the same lesson, at the same quality, for free.
